Businesses have the right to appeal a rating, to publish a reply alongside it, and to request a re-inspection once improvements have been made, so a rating listed here may since have changed. Each business's current rating is on the Food Standards Agency website.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Children and young people supported by social care in Rochdale will benefit from faster, simpler access to mental health and care support under a new Government pilot. Care Together will test and evaluate a new model of care, embedding mental health professionals from existing NHS services into children’s social care settings. The pilot aims to replace fragmented provision with faster access to expert, needs-led mental health support, including family therapy and support for parents and primary caregivers. The Government is investing up to £9.4 million over three years in the Care Together pilot, which will be run by Greater Manchester Integrated Care Board (ICB), working with Stockport, Tameside, and Rochdale local authorities. The pilot follows Professor Peter Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, which recommended better integrated mental health support. The latest figures on children in need, children on protection plans, children in care, and care leavers, including adopted children, across the three participating local authority areas show up to 7,000 children and young people, as well as their parents, carers, and/or guardians, will be covered by the pilot. By bringing social care and mental health professionals together in one team, children, young people, and their families will have faster access to support tailored to their needs, reducing the need to navigate multiple services. Dame Diana Johnson, Minister of State for Public Health and Patient Safety, said: “For too long, fragmented mental health services have left young people in care, care leavers, parents, carers, and guardians not knowing where to turn for support.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: As a new trial offering better mental health and social care support is launched in Rochdale, Minister of State for Public Health and Patient Safety Dame Diana Johnson tells the Rochdale Times how it will help young people and their families across the borough. “How many of us could have benefited from the understanding and guidance of a mental health professional while we were growing up? Growing up can be challenging for any child. Professor Peter Fonagy’s recent independent review of mental health conditions, ADHD and autism has highlighted the scale of the challenge. Mental health distress is rising, particularly among children and young people, with girls especially affected. Greater Manchester is not immune to this disturbing trend. For children already facing difficult circumstances, the health risks can be even greater. Children in contact with social services often have high levels of mental health need, alongside other challenges affecting their lives and wellbeing. That’s why I’m delighted Greater Manchester will lead the way in improving early mental health support for children through Care Together, a pilot designed to give children involved with social care services faster access to help. Backed by £6.4 million over three years, the programme will operate through NHS Pennine Trust, working with councils in Stockport, Tameside and Rochdale.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A special policing unit has been launched to keep road users and Bee Network passengers safe. The new policing model is intended to make the Bee Network one of the safest public transport networks in the world has been launched across Greater Manchester. The Transport Policing and Crime Command (TPACC) is a pioneering approach that will bring Greater Manchester Police (GMP), Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) even closer together to tackle crime, antisocial behaviour and road safety issues across the region’s transport network. Led by Chief Superintendent Suzanne Downey, the command will establish the Bee Network as GMP’s 11th policing district, which includes more than 60 new officers on the network, being supported by staff from TfGM all involved in keeping the network safe and providing greater reassurance to passengers. The dedicated unit has been formed with funding from the Mayor of Greater Manchester with an Operation Vulcan-style problem-solving approach to tackling crime and anti-social behaviour, making the Bee Network one of the safest public transport networks in the world. The unit will focus on crime and anti-social behaviour on the roads and transport network. Image: GMP As well as keeping passengers safe on buses, trams and active travel routes, it will also incorporate the existing Roads Policing Unit, the Commercial Vehicle Unit, the Serious Collision Investigation Unit and others. Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson said: “TPACC represents a significant step forward in how we police and protect Greater Manchester’s transport network.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: More than 350 guests came together at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday evening as the Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026 honoured the individuals and organisations transforming lives, creating opportunities and bringing communities together across the borough. Delivered by KYP (Kashmir Youth Project) since 2012, the awards recognised outstanding contributions to equality, diversity, inclusion and community cohesion. With finalists selected from more than 130 nominations, the evening showcased the very best of Rochdale and the people whose efforts make a positive difference every day. The evening brought together civic leaders, businesses, public sector organisations, charities, community groups and residents to celebrate the people and organisations whose dedication continues to break down barriers, create opportunities and strengthen communities. Zulf Ahmed, Chief Executive Officer of KYP, said: “The Rochdale Diversity Awards are about recognising the people and organisations whose commitment, compassion and leadership make a real difference to others every day. “This year we received more than 130 nominations, each telling a story of someone breaking down barriers, creating opportunities or helping others to thrive. Bringing together more than 350 guests to celebrate those achievements was incredibly special. Rochdale MP Paul Waugh with some of the winners. Image: Paul Waugh “The awards remind us of the strength of our communities and the extraordinary things that happen when people come together with a shared commitment to making Rochdale a fairer, more inclusive and more connected borough.” The audience also heard inspiring contributions from civic and community leaders from across the borough.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: The Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall and gardens will be hosting its popular fire festival once again later this winter and it’ll be free to attend. Built in 1871, the Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall is considered by Historic England to be ‘one of the finest municipal buildings in the country'. Just two years ago, the hall reopened following an ambitious restoration, which saw many of its original features repaired and has since been nominated for a number of awards. Earlier this year, Rochdale’s historic Broadfield Park Slopes, which sit between the Town Hall and St Chad’s Church, were also brought back to life with a restored fountain, new accessible pathways and improved landscaping. Click here for the latest on Manchester's food & drink scene, gigs and more in our CityLife newsletter The town hall and its gardens will take centre stage in one of the borough’s biggest winter events with the return of the popular Ignite Fire Festival, which will be held from November 20 to 22. Attended by around 10,000 people last year, the centrepiece of the 2026 event will consist of a light and fire trail featuring six walk-through zones all designed around the theme of the human body. The nighttime event, which will run from 5pm to 8pm across the three days, will mark the North West premiere of the ambitious fire and light installation, which has been created by Walk The Plank and has been shown in the likes of Ireland and Canada so far. Visitors will be able to walk through the ‘glowing embers’ of human metabolism and learn more about what keeps us alive through cutting-edge technology and dramatics. The attraction will also feature a Fire Garden consisting of illuminated slopes and gardens behind the Town Hall that will feature intricate hand-crafted fire sculptures and pyrotechnics. There will also be the 20-strong drumming collective Drum Machine, who will be bringing their lively, stomping tunes to proceedings. In addition, special Fireflies shows featuring mesmerising fire spinning from Rochdale’s Skylight Circus Arts and live fire shows by interactive arts group Travelling Light Circus. Each night, there will also be flame-cooked hot food on offer, as well as mulled wine and other seasonal drinks to enjoy. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, said: “Ignite Fire Festival has become a real success story for the borough, drawing audiences from across Greater Manchester and beyond. This 2026 line-up will build on that success with new attractions, creative performances and family-friendly experiences. It will be a fantastic celebration for residents and visitors alike, setting the stage perfectly for our Christmas lights switch-on.” Bev Ayre, senior producer at Walk the Plank, added: “The Body is unlike anything we’ve brought to Ignite before. An immersive fire and light experience that combines art, science and creativity to help people discover the incredible human body in a fun and engaging way. “Set against the stunning backdrop of Rochdale Town Hall Square and gardens, it promises to be one of our most exciting attractions yet. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Road closures and bus diversions remain in place on Portland Street following the burst water main Repairs to a burst water main and damaged road in Manchester city centre are likely to take several days, United Utilities has said. Piccadilly Gardens bus station and part of Portland Street remain closed for a second day following Wednesday's burst, with passengers directed to alternative bus stops. The water company said crews worked through the night to locate the burst while trying to maintain water supplies to nearby customers. Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) said trams to Bury, Rochdale and Ashton-under-Lyne continued to run normally from Piccadilly Gardens. A United Utilities spokesperson apologised for the inconvenience and said work would continue to repair the main as quickly as possible. "Due to the damage caused by the burst, it is likely that repairs and road reinstatement will take several days to complete," the spokesperson said. The company said it was working with TfGM and Manchester City Council to manage the disruption and reopen the road as soon as it was safe.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: The base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale has been completed, marking a major milestone in the development of Atom Valley’s advanced materials and manufacturing innovation district. Designed by Bond Bryan, the 30,000 sq. ft centre will provide a physical gateway into the UK’s advanced materials and manufacturing network, connecting businesses with specialist space, facilities, research expertise and support to help move new technologies from concept towards commercial application. The building is the first major physical development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub in Rochdale intended to bring together businesses, researchers, investors and innovation partners. The next phase will focus on specialist fit-out ahead of the centre becoming operational in 2027. The project addresses a key challenge for advanced manufacturing: creating environments that support the transition from research and development to commercialisation and production, while accommodating specialist processes and allowing for emerging technologies and changing business needs. Mark Adey, director at Bond Bryan, said: “The SMMC is about creating the infrastructure that allows innovation to move beyond the laboratory and into commercialisation and manufacture. That transition places very different demands on a building, so the challenge is creating highly technical environments that work for specialist processes today, while remaining flexible enough to respond to technologies and businesses that are still emerging. “We’ve spent decades designing research, science and advanced manufacturing environments across the UK, and that experience has shown us that the most successful places connect people, ideas and processes rather than treating research and production as separate worlds. SMMC brings those elements together in one place, creating an adaptable environment that can evolve alongside the industries it supports.” Rochdale Development Agency (RDA) has led the physical development of the centre, working with the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), The University of Manchester and wider innovation partners to secure investment and establish advanced materials and manufacturing as a priority for Rochdale and Greater Manchester. The project builds on the establishment of the Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) in 2023. Convened by RDA, CEAMS connects businesses with a national network of specialist expertise, facilities and innovation support, including The University of Manchester, the Henry Royce Institute, the National Physical Laboratory (NPL), the Centre for Process Innovation (CPI) and NCC, formerly the National Composites Centre.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A homeowner faces having to tear down a garden fence because of the impact it has on the neighbouring area. Rochdale Council refused Caterina Buonocore’s application for retrospective planning permission for the 1.55m high boundary fence — about twice the height of the original — around 19 Town House Road, Littleborough. She appealed that decision. But yesterday, a Planning Inspector rejected the appeal, stating: “The main issue is the effect of the appeal development on the character and appearance of the area. “Boundary treatments in the area are typically low-level and visually permeable, contributing to a sense of openness and allowing the soft landscaping within front gardens to remain appreciable. The existing greenery helps to soften the street scene and makes a positive contribution to the character and appearance of the area. “The appeal development introduces a close-boarded timber fence. The height, materials and extensive continuous form of enclosure contrasts with the more open and traditional forms of boundary treatment typically found in the locality. “On site, I observed that due to the prominent corner location, when seen from Park View against the back drop of traditional stone terraces with low-key forms of boundary treatment, the appeal development appears particularly stark and incongruous within the street scene. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Barry Jones was standing in the road when both drivers failed to stop Police have seized a car and a moped after their drivers failed to stop for a lollipop man on two separate occasions, forcing him to leap out of the way. Barry Jones was standing in Bury Old Road in Heywood, Greater Manchester, when the incidents happened on 13 and 14 October, Rochdale Borough Council said. The council said 137 incidents of drivers failing to stop for school crossing patrols had been reported across authority area over the past five years. Greater Manchester Police seized the silver Skoda car and moped after gathering evidence, including witness statements. The law was changed in June to remove the requirement for police to issue a warning before seizing vehicles under the Police Reform Act 2002. Barry Jones pictured helping pedestrians cross Bury Old Road Dylan Williams, cabinet member for highways, thanked police for their "quick and decisive action" and said the council would keep reporting incidents and push for prosecutions where possible.

This morning, 250 officers carried out a series of raids as part of Operation Rivercrest which is targeting an organised crime group. The operation led to the execution of 20 warrants – mostly in Rochdale and Heywood – as well as in areas across Bury, Salford, Manchester, Merseyside and Yorkshire. Those arrested range in age from 19 to 49. Sixteen men have been arrested on suspicion of various offences, including drugs supply, assault, violent disorder, affray, burglary, and robbery. One woman, aged 21, was arrested on suspicion of being concerned in the supply of drugs. DS Hannah Taala, of Greater Manchester Police’s Rochdale Division, said officers focused on the crime group after violence in Heywood earlier in the year . She said: “There was a large disorder in April, where multiple people were involved in violence in the Heywood area. “It ended in some quiet serious injuries, assaults, a stab wound, using vehicles in that disorder, weapons, machetes. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Foster carers who have between them clocked up a total of 465 years supporting children and young people across the borough have been recognised by Rochdale Council. A total of 34 fostering families were honoured at the council’s recent annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards at Rochdale Town Hall in gratitude for their outstanding commitment to providing safe, stable and nurturing homes for some of the most vulnerable. Between all the carers, it is estimated they have supported more than 1,020 children and young people from newborn to 18, while working with the local authority. Among those celebrating their individual milestones was Michael, aged 79, and Marilyn, aged 75, who are marking 50 years. Predominantly caring for newborn babies and siblings since 1976, the married couple from Milnrow have cared for more than 330 children in that time and are still welcoming youngsters into their home. Marilyn said: “We’ve been to their weddings, adoption parties, christenings, 18th and 21st birthday parties. “It’s lovely when you think you started off with them as a baby and now, they’ve grown. Ian and Carole McLean celebrate 40 years of fostering with Rochdale Council “We’ve had letters from adoptive parents saying, ‘They’ve turned out like they have because of you’ which is nice.”

candidates.source_body_excerpt: An album which is believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council has reached millions of listeners on national radio and streaming platforms. Kenion Street has enjoyed glowing reviews after being launched as part of Rochdale’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture. It features local acts performing their version of a classic track originally recorded at iconic studios in the town. From 1977 to 2001, Rochdale was home to both Suite Sixteen and Cargo Studios in Kenion Street, where trailblazing artists including OMD, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Joy Division, Inspiral Carpets, Autechre, A Certain Ratio, The Fall and many others recorded some of their most memorable work. The 11 tracks on Kenion Street included PoolEra’s version of Electricity by OMD, Dreams Never End by New Order re-imagined by Medley, and Jennifer Read’s dramatic version of Totally Wired, by The Fall. Micah Stalgic and choir Local Vocals performing Atmosphere by Joy Division, that features on the album All the new tracks were recorded and produced at Voltalab Sound Studios, based in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building in Kenion Street, by studio founder Jamie Alsop. Radio 6 Music also featured the album, playing Middleton band’s K-Estate’s version of Gang of Four’s Damaged Goods. It was also made Track of the Day on Radio X with other tracks played across XS Manchester, Mersey Radio, Phoenix FM and many more, with a combined audience of over 3.5 million.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A special topping out ceremony marked a major milestone in the construction of the Clegg Building at Hopwood Hall College. Being built by Willmott Dixon and funded by the Department for Education, Rochdale Council and the college, the landmark development is poised to become a modern and inspiring learning environment in the heart of Rochdale. The building was visited by Principal and CEO Julia Heap OBE, Rochdale Member of Parliament Paul Waugh, the Mayor and Mayoress of Rochdale, Faisal Rana and Iram Faisal, among others. Members of the family of the late Robert Clegg OBE, in whose honour the new building has been named, joined as special guests for the event. Robert served as Chair of the Corporation at Hopwood Hall College from 2007 to 2018, making a significant contribution to the college during his time in the role. Robert’s wife Anne, son Richard and daughter Emma attended the ceremony to mark the occasion, with Emma continuing the family’s connection to the college as a current part-time adult learner. During the ceremony, the team from Willmott Dixon led visitors to the roof of the structure, which offers sweeping views of the borough, including Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Parish Church. There was then an opportunity for visitors to leave a message on part of the roof parapet in what will now become a permanent record of the occasion.

An eight-year-old school pupil has won a competition to name a road for a new £6.4 million First Choice Homes Development in Heywood. Ava McEvoy put forward the name Murphy Close for the housing association’s 27-home Bury Old Road project in honour of a local Catholic priest. Father Morris Murphy founded a parish for the Darnhill Estate in the 1960s and was a respected community figure until his death in 2013. Ava, who goes to Our Lady and St Paul's RC Primary School, received a Samsung tablet for her winning name. "I'm really happy that my street name was chosen," she said. "I picked Murphy Close because Father Murphy did so much for the local community, and I wanted people to remember him." Headteacher of Ava’s school, Hollie Aspinall added: "We are incredibly proud of Ava and all the pupils who took part in the competition.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A nursery has lost its bid to keep a caravan which replaced a temporary Portakabin in its yard. Little Oaks Nursery applied to Rochdale Council for retrospective planning permission for the caravan which is being used as an outbuilding at its site in Bamford Road, Heywood. It follows planning permission granted in 2022 for a temporary Portakabin classroom which was removed in 2024. A planning officer’s report said: “Simultaneously, pre-application advice was requested and given for the siting of a static caravan on the site. “The advice given was that such a structure would not be visually appropriate for the site and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. “Notwithstanding, it appears that a static caravan was nonetheless placed at the site without the benefit of planning permission and this application therefore seeks regulation of such. “The caravan does not provide the high-quality design that officers had previously stated would be required for a permanent structure. “In design terms, the caravan is of no visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaces, which was accepted only for a temporary period on the basis that it was unacceptable for permanent retention.

This year’s category win keeps the title in the borough after Middleton town centre took the top prize last year. Rochdale has undergone significant regeneration in recent years. The Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall has been expertly restored, complemented by the creation of the new Town Hall Square and the transformation of the Broadfield Park slopes. Supported by a multi-million-pound National Lottery Heritage Fund grant, have made this historic quarter the envy of many. Judges praised Rochdale town centre’s vibrant displays from Bowlee Garden Nursery, recycling initiatives and exceptional cleanliness, as well as the pride, teamwork and dedication of everyone involved. They also recognised the commitment to local biodiversity and strong partnerships, with Rochdale exceeding the gold standard in horticulture, environmental responsibility and community participation. Rochdale’s historic Baillie Street Quarter and striking murals, created through the 2025 Rochdale Common Walls Festival, strengthened the town centre’s entry by showcasing its culture and civic pride. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Renovating Rochdale’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks would force residents out of their homes for more than a decade, housing chiefs have said. While Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says no decision on the future of the landmark College Bank blocks has been taken, residents have asked new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig to back their campaign to refurbish their homes rather than demolish them. But if campaigners get their wish, the scale of bringing the 61-year-old buildings up to modern standards would take more than 10 years and they could not be occupied until the work is complete, RBH chiefs have said. Members of Greater Manchester Tenants Union recently met Ms Craig to discuss the steps that could be taken to renovate almost 1,000 homes in College Bank and Lower Falinge. Plans to demolish College Bank were first discussed in 2017 when RBH warned that the buildings were approaching the end of their life. Tenants set up the Save the Seven Sisters campaign and hoped RBH’s partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the towers restored. But in September, 2024, it was announced that the partnership would not continue. The union and the Save the Seven Sisters campaign asked then Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to help. In November, 2024, the Mayoral Taskforce was established to look at the options for the College Bank estate. Rochdale’s skyline without the Seven Sisters towers. Image: Copilot In October 2025, RBH announced the results of surveys which found the blocks were not safe to remain occupied and residents would be required to leave their homes.
